findings.title: KeyError when integration metadata has no "sender" entry
findings.body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing `Integration` row carries a `sender` key in its metadata. `build_integration()` (line 376) only stores `sender` when the pipeline state contains it, and the pipeline itself never binds a `sender` key, so any Integration created/updated by the installation pipeline (as opposed to the GitHub `installation` webhook) has metadata without `sender`. If such an Integration exists while the OrganizationIntegration does not (e.g. the org integration was deleted and the user re-runs the install), this line raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly what to do when the sender is unknown.

findings.title: GitHub user validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet
findings.body: The new ownership check only runs on the code path where an `Integration` row for `installation_id` already exists. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised (line 481) the pipeline advances immediately and `build_integration()` resolves the installation purely with the app JWT, which does not prove the current user owns that installation. Since the `Integration` row is created asynchronously by the GitHub `installation` webhook, a user who supplies someone else's `installation_id` before the webhook is processed (or if the webhook never arrives) can still attach that installation to their own Sentry org — the exact scenario this PR intends to block. Consider validating the authenticated GitHub login against the installation account/sender fetched from `get_installation_info()` instead of relying solely on previously stored metadata.

findings.title: Network failures during token exchange and user lookup produce a 500 instead of the error page
findings.body: `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the `try` block, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `resp.raise_for_status()` internally. Any transport error, timeout, or non-2xx response from GitHub therefore propagates out of `dispatch()` and results in an unhandled exception/500 for the user, instead of the `error(request, self.active_organization)` page used for every other failure in this view. Wrap both calls and return the standard error response.

findings.title: Authorize URL built by string interpolation without URL-encoding parameters
findings.body: The GitHub authorize URL is assembled with an f-string, so `state` and especially `redirect_uri` (built from `absolute_uri`, which depends on the deployment's URL prefix) are inserted into the query string unencoded. If the URL prefix ever contains characters that must be percent-encoded (`?`, `&`, `#`, non-ASCII, a path with a query), the resulting authorize request is malformed and the OAuth step will fail or redirect somewhere unexpected. Build the query with `urlencode({...})`.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 installation error
findings.body: The assertion was changed from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`, which is the message emitted by the new OAuth/state failure branch (`error()` default), not by `build_integration()`'s `IntegrationError` for a missing installation. Combined with the hand-written `state` value (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, different from every other test), the test now passes without ever reaching `get_installation_info()`, so the 404-installation path that the test is named for is no longer exercised. Either keep asserting the specific message after a valid OAuth step, or add a separate test for the state-mismatch branch.

findings.title: Brittle positional assertion on responses.calls index
findings.body: `responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` hard-codes the position of the app-installations request in the recorded call list, which now depends on the exact number and ordering of the new OAuth calls (`/login/oauth/access_token`, `/user`). Any future change in the pipeline's request order silently asserts the wrong request (or raises IndexError). Match on the request URL instead of the index.
